title: Memory allocation: malloc, arenas and why RSS grows
goal: By the end, you can explain how malloc gets memory from the kernel and hands it out, why memory a program frees usually stays in its RSS, what glibc's arenas trade for speed, and how to account for a Java program's memory with NMT.
opening:
The café buys its milk by the crate from a wholesaler, and pours it a cup at a time. Leftover milk goes into the café's own fridge, not back to the wholesaler. After a busy Saturday, the fridge is still full on a quiet Monday.

Programs get memory the same way. The program that records the café's card payments has a busy hour, and afterwards it holds 300 MB more memory than at start-up. The number stays there for days, though the program has freed almost everything it used. It looks like a leak, and the first idea is to give it more memory.

It's easy to believe that freeing memory gives it back to the computer. The word itself suggests it.

In Copy-on-write, mmap and the OOM killer, we saw that the Java heap is only part of what the kernel counts. In this lesson, we'll open up the rest: how programs get memory in bulk, why freed memory stays, and how to account for every megabyte. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A C program (C is a language that runs close to the hardware) asks for 200,000 blocks of 1,000 bytes with `malloc`, about 192 MB in all. Then it frees every block except the one it asked for last. What happens to the amount of memory the computer shows it using?
options: It drops to a few MB: freeing hands the memory back to the computer
It stays at about 195 MB
It halves, because the memory goes back in big steps
It drops at the next garbage collection
warmup.why: `free` returns blocks to `malloc`'s own lists, not to the kernel (the core of the operating system, which hands memory to programs). The program's heap can shrink only from its top end, and the one block still in use at the top holds all 192 MB of free blocks below it in place. In the lab box, RSS (the program's memory in RAM) stayed at 195 MB until that last block was freed too, then fell to 2 MB at once. The last option is a Java habit: C has no garbage collector, the part of a language that frees unused memory by itself.

sections.h: How malloc buys memory in bulk and hands it out in pieces
sections.body:
Let's price a request to the kernel first. The kernel is the core of the operating system, and a system call is a request a program makes to it. `mmap` and `munmap` are the system calls that hand out memory and take it back, a page at a time (a page is 4 KB, the unit the kernel hands memory out in). `bulk.c` asks for one page with `mmap`, writes to it and gives it back with `munmap`, 100,000 times. Each round costs about 6 to 11 µs (millionths of a second) in the lab box. Then it does the same with `malloc` and `free`, for 64 bytes. That round costs about 20 ns (billionths of a second). That's a factor of several hundred, and a Java program, a database or a C library asks for small pieces of memory millions of times.

So `malloc` isn't a system call. It's a function in the C library, the code almost every program on Linux uses (glibc's version, in the lab box). You call `malloc(n)` and get back the address of a block of n bytes, the number that says where in memory the block starts. `free` hands the block back. Inside, the library gets memory from the kernel in big pieces and hands it out in small ones. In café terms, the kernel is the wholesaler, `malloc` pours by the cup, and the library's own lists are the café's fridge.

Let's build an allocator, the code behind `malloc`, starting with the simplest one that works: a bump pointer. The library takes a big region of memory (a range of addresses) and keeps a pointer (a variable that holds an address) to its first unused byte. Each `malloc(n)` returns that pointer and moves it forward by n bytes. When the region runs out, the library asks the kernel for more. On Linux, the classic way to ask is `brk`, a system call that moves the end of the heap, the region where malloc's blocks live. That end is called the **program break**. Bump allocation is as fast as allocation gets, but it has no `free`. A program that takes and frees a 1 KB buffer for each request would grow by 1 KB per request, forever.

So the allocator has to remember what was freed. glibc stores an 8-byte size field just before each block, and the block and its header together are a **chunk**. `free(p)` reads the size and puts the chunk on a free list, a list of chunks ready for reuse. `malloc(n)` looks for a free chunk that fits, and splits off what it doesn't need. Two free chunks side by side merge into one, so three neighbouring 1,000-byte holes can serve a 3,000-byte request. The free space after the last chunk, up to the break, is the **top chunk**. When nothing on the free lists fits, `malloc` cuts the block from the top chunk. When that runs out, it calls `brk` again and takes 128 KB extra, so the next hundred small requests need no system call.

Big requests take another road. A chunk of 128 KB or more that doesn't fit gets its own `mmap`, and `free` hands it straight back with `munmap`. That's the only memory that leaves the program the moment it's freed. glibc then raises that 128 KB threshold to the size of the block it just freed (up to 32 MB), betting that the program will ask for that size again.

The trace of `sizes.c` shows all of it. The first `malloc(1000)` moves the break up by 135,168 bytes: the chunk plus 128 KB, rounded up to whole pages of 4 KB. Another 1,000 bytes and a 100 KB block come from the top chunk, with no system call. 200 KB and 1 MB get their own `mmap`. Freeing the 1 MB block unmaps it. The next 1 MB request, now under the raised threshold, grows the heap with `brk` instead.

Real glibc doesn't search one long list. It sorts free chunks into bins by size. And since glibc 2.26, each thread (one line of work inside a program) also has a small cache of its own, the tcache. It keeps up to 7 freed chunks per size, for sizes up to 1,032 bytes, and reuses them without waiting for any other thread.

So `malloc` is fast because it rarely calls the kernel. Next, we'll see the price: memory you free doesn't go back to the kernel.

try.title: Price a system call per allocation, then watch malloc's calls
steps: Start the lab box from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box`. The lab box is a small Linux machine that runs in Docker (a program that runs separate small machines, called containers, on your computer), and your `labs` folder appears inside it as `/labs`. `gcc` is the C compiler: it turns the source code into a program you can run.

`os/c/l08/bulk.c` times one-page `mmap` + write + `munmap` against `malloc` + write + `free`. `os/c/l08/sizes.c` asks for 1,000 bytes twice, then 100 KB, 200 KB and 1 MB. It frees the 1 MB block and asks for 1 MB again, and prints a marker line before each step.

Predict which steps of `sizes.c` make a system call, and which call. Then run the block. `strace` prints every system call a program makes, and `-e trace=` picks which ones. The `sed` drops the program's start-up and keeps the lines from the first marker on.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
gcc -O2 -o /tmp/bulk os/c/l08/bulk.c && /tmp/bulk
gcc -O2 -o /tmp/sizes os/c/l08/sizes.c
strace -o /tmp/sizes.txt -e trace=brk,mmap,munmap,write /tmp/sizes > /dev/null
sed -n '/malloc 1000 bytes/,$p' /tmp/sizes.txt

sections.h: Why freed memory stays: free gives it back to malloc, not to the kernel
sections.body:
`frag.c` asks for 200,000 blocks of 1,000 bytes, about 192 MB of heap. Its RSS (resident set size, the amount of its memory that sits in RAM) reaches 195 MB. Then it frees 97% of the blocks, keeping one in every 32. RSS stays at 195 MB.

Nothing leaked. A leak is memory a program forgets to free, and `frag.c` freed it. `free` gave every chunk back to `malloc`, which merged the neighbours into free chunks of about 31 KB and keeps them for the next `malloc`. What `free` doesn't do is give pages back to the kernel, and two things stand in the way. The stepper shows both on a small heap.

The first is the shape of the heap. `brk` only moves the end of one unbroken region, so the heap can shrink only from the top. glibc does shrink it: when the top chunk grows past 128 KB (the setting `M_TRIM_THRESHOLD`), `free` moves the break down and keeps 128 KB spare. But one block still in use near the top holds everything below it in place. Run `frag.c` keeping only the very last block, and RSS still stays at 195 MB, with 192 MB of free chunks under that one block. Free the last block too, and RSS drops to 2 MB at once.

The second is that the pages of a free chunk still sit in RAM, and still hold data. To give back a page from the middle of the heap, the allocator must tell the kernel it no longer needs what's in it. The system call for that is `madvise`, with `MADV_DONTNEED`. The address stays valid, and the frame behind it, the 4 KB piece of real RAM, goes back to the kernel. The next touch gets a fresh page of zeros (the first-touch fault of Virtual memory). glibc does this only when the program calls `malloc_trim(0)`. It walks every free chunk and gives back each whole page inside it, keeping the chunk's first 48 bytes, where the free list's pointers live. In `frag.c`, each free run of about 31 KB holds 6 or 7 whole pages. So RSS falls from 195 MB to 33 MB, while the heap still spans 192 MB of addresses.

This is **fragmentation**: free memory broken into pieces. `malloc` can reuse a piece for a block that fits, but the kernel can't take back a page that shares its 4 KB with a block still in use. Here the café picture breaks. A café could hand back any amount of leftover milk, if the wholesaler allowed it. The kernel takes memory back only in whole 4 KB pages, and one small block in use keeps its whole page.

A program that runs for days, builds a big structure and then keeps a few survivors looks exactly like `frag.c`. RSS climbs to the peak and stays near it, though the program has freed most of what it asked for. That's the opening's 300 MB: a peak, kept and reused by later requests. A real leak looks different: under steady work, it keeps climbing and never levels off. **Freed memory goes back to malloc, not to the kernel. Judge a leak by its growth, not its size.**

One heap is the easy case. A program with many threads gets more than one, and the next section counts what that costs.

refs.title: malloc(3): notes on arenas and brk

aside.title: Why can't malloc move the blocks together?
aside.body: Because the program holds their addresses. A C program keeps the raw address that `malloc` returned, often in many places, and nothing tells `malloc` where those copies are. If it moved a block, every copy of that address would point at the wrong bytes. Java's garbage collector can move objects, because Java code never sees a raw address: the JVM knows every reference and fixes them all when it moves an object. That's how a Java heap can pack its survivors together, and a C heap can't.

sections.h: Arenas: one heap per thread, and one peak per heap
sections.body:
`arenas.c` starts 16 threads. One at a time, each one asks for 16 MB in 4,000-byte blocks and frees all but its last block. With glibc's defaults, the program ends with RSS 253 MB. With the setting `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1`, it ends with 17 MB. Same program, same frees.

The reason is a lock. A lock lets only one thread at a time change something shared, and makes the others wait their turn. A heap with free lists is shared, so `malloc` and `free` must hold a lock while they change it. With a single heap, threads that ask for memory at the same moment queue for that lock. In one run of the same program, 16 threads each did 200,000 `malloc` and `free` pairs. That took 1.4 s with one heap, and 0.18 s with glibc's defaults.

glibc's answer is more heaps. An **arena** is a complete heap with its own lock, its own free lists and its own top chunk. The main thread uses the main arena, the `brk` heap. Any other thread gets an arena at its first `malloc`: a new one while there are fewer than the limit, and after that a share of an existing one. The limit is 8 per CPU on 64-bit Linux, so 96 on the lab box's 12 CPUs. A thread keeps the arena it got. Extra arenas live in their own regions from `mmap`, and each one reserves 64 MB of addresses. VSZ, the virtual size (all the address space a program has reserved, used or not), was 1,155 MB with 17 arenas and 146 MB with one.

The price is that free memory belongs to an arena. When thread 1 frees its 16 MB, the chunks go back on its arena's free lists. Thread 2, asking from a different arena, can't reuse them. Each arena keeps its own peak, so 16 threads that each needed 16 MB at a different moment end up holding 16 × 16 MB. With one arena, each thread reuses the chunks the previous one freed, and the program holds one peak. The café would have the same trade with one fridge per cook. Nobody queues at a fridge door, but every fridge fills with its own cook's leftovers, and no cook can use another's.

`MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` sets the limit through the environment, the list of settings a program reads when it starts, so it must be set before the program starts. For a Java program with hundreds of threads that each call C code now and then, a small value such as 2 or 4 is worth trying. It costs more waiting on arena locks, which matters only if the program calls `malloc` very often: here 2 arenas gave 33 MB and 0.21 s. Another way out is a different allocator. jemalloc and tcmalloc are two other `malloc` libraries. `LD_PRELOAD`, a setting that tells Linux to load a library first, puts one in place of glibc's, and each makes its own choices about when to give memory back.

Arenas explain a C program's memory. A Java program adds a layer on top, and a tool that sees only part of it. That's next.

```text
16 x 200000 malloc+free pairs at once: 205 ms
each thread built and freed 16 MB in turn: arenas 2, RSS 33 MB, VSZ 210 MB
MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1, 16 threads
16 x 200000 malloc+free pairs at once: 1392 ms
each thread built and freed 16 MB in turn: arenas 1, RSS 17 MB, VSZ 146 MB
```

17 arenas is the main one plus one per thread, each holding its thread's 16 MB peak. Two arenas hold two peaks, and one arena holds one. VSZ drops by about 1 GB, 64 MB for each extra arena's reservation. The 1,392 ms is the lock: 16 threads queueing for one heap.

sections.h: A Java program's memory: the heap, the rest, and what NMT can't see
sections.body:
`NativeChurn` is a Java program. It runs on the JVM (Java virtual machine), the program that runs Java code, with a 64 MB heap. It touches every heap page up front, so the whole heap is in RAM from the start (`-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch`, from Virtual memory). Then 16 threads take turns. Each creates 64 `java.util.zip.Deflater` objects, Java's tool for compressing data, and ends all but one. The JVM's own accounting says it holds 145 MB. The kernel says the program has 309 MB of anonymous memory (memory that belongs to no file) in RAM.

A JVM gets all its memory from `mmap` and `malloc`, like any other program. The Java heap, where Java objects live, is one big `mmap`, reserved at the size of `-Xmx`, the heap's limit. Around it sit the other parts. Metaspace holds what the JVM knows about loaded classes. The code cache holds Java code the JVM has turned into machine code, the instructions the CPU runs directly, while the program runs. Every thread has a stack, and the garbage collector (the part of the JVM that frees objects nothing uses) keeps its own records. Then come many smaller `malloc`s for the JVM's own bookkeeping. When RSS is bigger than the heap, the question is which of these it is.

**Native Memory Tracking** (NMT) answers that for the JVM's own parts. Native memory means memory outside the Java heap. Start the JVM with `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`, which the documentation from Oracle (the company behind Java) says costs 5 to 10% in speed. Then `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary` prints one line per part. (`jcmd` sends commands to a running JVM, and the pid is its process number.) Each line has `reserved`, address space like VSZ, and `committed`, memory the JVM has made ready to use. Committed is the most that can be in RAM. A committed heap page that was never touched isn't in RSS, which is why this demo touches its heap up front.

NMT counts what HotSpot, the JVM itself, asks for, and nothing else. Its documentation says so: it doesn't track memory that other C code allocates, including the C code behind Java's own built-in classes. Each `Deflater` holds the working state of zlib, a compression library written in C. That's about 260 KB, which zlib gets from `malloc` in the calling thread. So 1,024 of them went through 16 arenas, and NMT saw none of it. Ending them freed the chunks into their arenas, which kept them, as the last section showed. The same goes for any Java library that calls C code through JNI, Java's way of calling C.

So read a Java program's memory in three layers. RSS, split into `RssAnon` (anonymous memory) and `RssFile` (pages of files), is what the kernel and a container's limit count. NMT's committed total is what the JVM itself accounts for. The difference is C code outside the JVM, plus memory the allocator kept after `free`: about 160 MB here. Setting `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` cut RSS from 320 MB to 145 MB, and NMT's numbers didn't change at all. **When RSS and NMT disagree, the gap is outside the JVM. Look at the allocator before the heap.**

Everything in this lesson is memory that programs asked for. The kernel also fills RAM on its own, with copies of files, and that's where the next lesson goes.

try.title: NMT against RSS, with and without many arenas
steps: `NativeChurn` runs 16 threads in turn. Each creates 64 `Deflater` objects, compresses 64 KB with each, and ends all but one. The block runs it twice with NMT on: first with glibc's default arenas, then with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, which `env` puts in the JVM's environment.
Predict which numbers move between the two runs: NMT's committed total, `RssAnon`, or both. Then run it in the lab box. It takes about 15 seconds.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l08/demo/NativeChurn.java
for setting in "" MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2; do
  env $setting java -Xms64m -Xmx64m -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary \
    -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l08.demo.NativeChurn 16 5 & pid=$!
  sleep 3
  jcmd $pid VM.native_memory summary scale=MB | grep -E '^Total|^ +malloc:'
  grep -E '^(RssAnon|RssFile)' /proc/$pid/status
  wait $pid
done

compare.title: pmap -x of the same JVM: glibc's default arenas against MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2
compare.note: `pmap -x` lists a program's memory regions, with how much of each is in RAM. Both lists show the 62 MB Java heap at `0xfc000000`. On the left, sixteen arenas sit at addresses that end in `000000`, 64 MB apart, each holding 13 MB of zlib memory that was freed but kept. On the right there are two: the `brk` heap (the `0xaaaa...` address, next to the program's own code) and one extra arena, each holding about one thread's peak. VSZ falls from 4.5 GB to 1.8 GB, and RSS from 327 MB to 148 MB. Nothing in the Java code changed.

lab.title: Build glibc-style malloc and free, then arenas
steps: Open the three captured files: the `sizes.c` trace and the `frag.c` and `arenas.c` runs from this lesson. The tests replay each one on your model. They check for the same system calls in the same order, RSS within a megabyte or two, and the same number of arenas.

Read `Malloc.kt`. `Sizes` holds glibc's sizes. In `Heap`, the free chunks live in `freeChunks` (address to size, in address order) and chunks in use in `used`. `trim`, `shrink`, `grow`, `mmapChunk`, `unmap` and `touch` are written for you.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All seven fail for now.
Write `Heap.malloc` in the four steps its KDoc (the comment above the function) lists: first fit with a split, the top chunk, `mmapChunk`, `grow`.
Write `Heap.free`. Either unmap the chunk, or merge it with the free neighbours on both sides. Then it either joins the top chunk (and maybe calls `shrink(topPad)`) or goes back in `freeChunks`.
Write `Arenas.arenaFor`. Then look at the arena test's three runs side by side: the same frees, and three very different RSS figures.
hints: `freeChunks.entries.firstOrNull { it.value >= size }` is first fit (the first free chunk that's big enough), because a `TreeMap` goes through its keys in address order.
The top chunk is too small when `brk - top < size + Sizes.MIN_CHUNK`. Only then do you choose between `mmapChunk` (size at or over `mmapThreshold`) and `grow`.

In `free`, the chunk after yours starts at `start + size`, so `freeChunks.remove(start + size)` merges it in one call. The chunk before is `freeChunks.lowerEntry(start)`, but only if it ends exactly at `start`.
If the merged chunk ends at `top`, move `top` down to its start and don't add it to `freeChunks`. Call `shrink(topPad)` when `brk - top >= trimThreshold`.

drill.title: Predict malloc's system calls

answer.src:
char *a = malloc(64);           // brk +132 KB: the first chunk plus 128 KB of top pad
char *b = malloc(64 * 1024);    // none: 64 KB fits in the top chunk
char *c = malloc(512 * 1024);   // mmap of 516 KB: over the 128 KB threshold, too big for the top
free(c);                        // munmap; the threshold rises to 516 KB
char *d = malloc(512 * 1024);   // brk: now under the threshold, and the top chunk is too small

recap: `malloc` is a library function, not a system call. It gets memory from the kernel in bulk with `brk` (moving the program break) or `mmap`, and hands it out in chunks, each with a size header.

Freed chunks go on malloc's free lists and merge with free neighbours. Requests of 128 KB or more that don't fit get their own `mmap` and go back to the kernel on `free`; glibc then raises that threshold.
The `brk` heap shrinks only from the top, so one block still in use can hold megabytes of free chunks in RAM. `malloc_trim(0)` gives whole free pages back from the middle with `madvise`.
glibc gives threads separate arenas (up to 8 per CPU) so they don't queue for one lock. Each arena keeps its own freed memory, so RSS can hold one peak per arena. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` caps them.

A Java program's RSS is the heap plus metaspace, the code cache, stacks, the garbage collector's records and C libraries' memory. NMT shows the JVM's own part; the rest is C code outside the JVM and memory the allocator kept.
The limit: a peak that stays is reuse, and steady growth is a leak, but no single number tells them apart. Only watching RSS over time under steady work does.
closing:
We started with a café fridge that stays full after a busy Saturday, and a program that keeps 300 MB after its busy hour. `malloc` buys memory in bulk, `free` puts it back in malloc's own fridge, and every arena keeps its own leftovers.

On a Linux machine, run `pmap -x` with a program's process number, and look for many anonymous regions 64 MB apart: one per arena. For a Java program, compare its RSS with NMT's committed total.

Next, we'll meet the memory the kernel fills on its own, the page cache, and find out why a write that succeeded may still not be on the disk.

quiz.q: From Virtual memory: right after `/tmp/frag 32` calls `malloc_trim(0)`, its heap still spans 192 MB of addresses, but RSS is 33 MB. What happened to the other pages?
options: They were written to swap, an area of the disk for pages pushed out of RAM
The kernel took back their frames. The addresses still belong to the program, and touching one again takes a minor fault and gets a page of zeros
They were compacted: malloc moved the blocks still in use closer together
They still hold their data, but `ps` stops counting pages that are free in malloc
quiz.why: `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` removes the page-table entries (the kernel's notes of where each page sits in RAM) and frees the frames, but leaves the region in place. The next access is a first touch again: a minor fault, one the kernel handles without the disk, that maps a frame of zeros. Nothing went to disk. And C's malloc can't move blocks in use, because the program holds their raw addresses. The first option is tempting, but swap would keep the data, and here the data is gone.

quiz.q: A program asks `malloc` for a 64 KB buffer for each request and frees it when the request ends. After a busy hour, its RSS stays 300 MB higher than at start-up, then stays flat for days under steady work. What's the most likely cause?
options: A memory leak in the code that handles requests
The kernel forgot to take the pages back
Freed chunks kept in malloc's free lists and arenas at the busy hour's peak, and reused by later requests
The 64 KB buffers come from `mmap` and are never unmapped
quiz.why: 64 KB is under the 128 KB mmap threshold, so the buffers come from heaps that keep their freed chunks. RSS rises to the peak and stays there, and later requests reuse the chunks, so it doesn't grow further. A leak would keep growing under steady work, which is why the first option fails. A block from `mmap` would go back to the kernel on `free`.

quiz.q: A Java program with 300 threads runs on a virtual machine with 4 CPUs. Its threads use a compression library written in C now and then. With default settings, how many glibc arenas can that library's `malloc` calls end up spread over?
options: 1: the JVM has a single C heap
4: one per CPU
300: one per thread
Up to 32: 8 per CPU on 64-bit Linux, after which threads share
quiz.why: glibc creates a new arena at a thread's first `malloc` until it reaches 8 per CPU on 64-bit Linux, then hands out existing ones. In a container limited only by a share of CPU time, glibc still counts the host's CPUs, so the limit can be much higher. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` sets it outright. The third option is tempting, because each thread does get its own arena at first, but only up to the limit.

quiz.q: NMT's committed total for a Java program stays at 600 MB for a day, while its RSS climbs from 700 MB to 1.4 GB. Where should you look first?
options: At memory outside the JVM: C libraries' `malloc` and what the allocator keeps after `free`, for example with `pmap -x` and `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX`
At the Java heap: take a heap dump
At metaspace: classes are leaking
Nowhere: NMT is the true number, and RSS counts too much
quiz.why: NMT tracks only the JVM's own memory, heap and metaspace included, and that's flat. The growth is in memory NMT can't see: C libraries such as zlib, and freed chunks that glibc keeps. RSS is what the kernel and a container's limit count, so it's the number that gets the program killed. That's why the last option fails.

quiz.q: A C program asks for a 2 MB buffer for each batch of work and frees it afterwards. `strace`, a tool that prints every system call a program makes, shows `mmap` and `munmap` for the first batch and one `brk` for the second. From the third batch on, there are no system calls at all. Why?
options: The kernel keeps the last unmapped region ready for the program
Freeing the 2 MB block raised glibc's mmap threshold above 2 MB, so later buffers come from the heap and are reused there
strace stops tracing after the first call of each kind
glibc maps 2 MB with huge pages, which strace can't see
quiz.why: glibc's threshold moves. Freeing a block from `mmap` that's bigger than the threshold (and at most 32 MB) raises the threshold to that block's size. The next 2 MB request is under it, so it grows the heap once with `brk`. After that, each `free` and `malloc` reuses the same chunk without calling the kernel. The first option sounds likely, but the kernel keeps nothing for the program after `munmap`.

flashcards.back: It moves the program break, the end of the program's heap. glibc's main arena grows and shrinks the heap with it.

flashcards.front: When does glibc use `mmap` for a single `malloc`?
flashcards.back: When the chunk is at least the mmap threshold (128 KB at first, raised up to 32 MB as big blocks are freed) and doesn't fit in the free lists or the top chunk.

flashcards.front: Why can RSS stay high after `free`?
flashcards.back: Freed chunks stay on malloc's free lists, and the `brk` heap shrinks only from the top. Only whole free pages at the top, or those `malloc_trim` hands back, return to the kernel.
It gives back every whole page inside free chunks (with `madvise`) and trims the top of the heap. The addresses stay; the RAM goes.

flashcards.front: What is a glibc arena, and what's the default limit?
flashcards.back: A separate heap with its own lock and free lists, so threads don't queue for one. The default limit is 8 per CPU on 64-bit Linux; `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` changes it.
Memory that C code outside the JVM allocates (JDK libraries such as zlib, and libraries called through JNI), and memory glibc keeps after `free`.

terms.plain: The end of a program's heap. The `brk` system call moves it up or down.
A block handed out by malloc plus its hidden size header: the unit malloc splits, frees and merges.
The free space at the end of a heap, up to the break, that malloc cuts from when its free lists have nothing that fits.
Free memory broken into pieces: too small for a request, or sharing pages with blocks in use, so the kernel can't take them back.
One of glibc's separate heaps, each with its own lock, so threads don't all wait for one.
The size from which glibc gives a request its own region from `mmap` instead of cutting it from a heap.
Native Memory Tracking: the JVM's own count of its memory outside the Java heap, part by part, read with jcmd.

explain_back.prompt: A friend's Java program shows 1.4 GB of RSS with `-Xmx512m`. NMT says about 700 MB committed, and RSS never comes down after the morning's busy hour. They want to raise the memory limit and call it a leak. Explain what's going on, and what you'd try first.
explain_back.answer: The heap is only one part of what the kernel counts. NMT's 700 MB covers the JVM's own memory: the 512 MB heap plus metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks and the garbage collector's records. The other 700 MB is memory the JVM didn't ask for itself, so NMT can't see it. That's C libraries the program calls, such as compression or database drivers written in C, and very often glibc keeping memory after `free`. glibc gives each thread an arena, up to 8 per CPU, and freed chunks go back to their arena's free lists, not to the kernel. A heap can shrink only from the top, so each arena holds on to its own peak. That's why RSS rises to the morning's peak and then stays flat: the memory is reused, not leaked. A leak would keep climbing under steady work. I'd check `pmap -x` for many anonymous regions on 64 MB boundaries. I'd take an NMT baseline, and a `summary.diff` later, to show that the JVM's own parts are flat. Then I'd set `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` in the program's environment and compare RSS under the same load. Raising the limit only hides it until the next peak.

deeper.body:
The tcache that glibc added in 2.26 is a per-thread array of 64 lists, one per 16-byte size class up to 1,032 bytes, each holding up to 7 freed chunks. A `free` of a small block puts it on its thread's list without a lock, and the next `malloc` of the same size takes it right back. That's why `bulk.c`'s 64-byte `malloc` and `free` cost about 20 ns. It's also why `arenas.c` uses 4,000-byte blocks: smaller ones would never reach the arena's lock.

The arena heaps are visible in `/proc/<pid>/maps`, the kernel's list of a program's regions. glibc reserves each one as a 64 MB region lined up on a 64 MB boundary. It makes the region inaccessible (`---p`) except for the part in use, and opens more of it up with `mprotect` as the arena grows. That's the `16776` KB `rw---` region at each 64 MB boundary in the `pmap` output above; the rest of the 64 MB is the reserved part. The alignment lets `free` find a chunk's arena from its address alone, by rounding down to 64 MB.

glibc's limits can be changed without rebuilding the program. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX`, `MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_`, `MALLOC_TOP_PAD_` and `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_` (note the trailing underscores on the last three) map to the `mallopt` parameters, and newer glibc versions read the same settings as tunables through `GLIBC_TUNABLES`. Setting any of the last three switches the moving mmap threshold off.

The JVM can show you the allocator's side too. `jcmd <pid> System.native_heap_info` prints glibc's `malloc_info` report, with one `<heap nr=...>` element per arena, the same report `arenas.c` counts. `jcmd <pid> System.trim_native_heap` makes glibc run `malloc_trim` inside a live JVM, which is a quick test of how much of RSS is free chunks. On a `NativeChurn` JVM started without NMT, it printed `Trim native heap: RSS+Swap: 262M->61652K (-202M)`: 200 MB that only looked like a leak.

Libraries that a Java program calls through JNI, such as RocksDB (a storage library written in C++) or compression libraries, allocate with `malloc` in whichever thread calls them. They behave like `NativeChurn` here: their memory lands in glibc's arenas, and NMT doesn't see it.
